review.title: Peribiliary glands and cysts
review.text: Peribiliary glands sit in and around the walls of larger bile ducts. Cysts of peribiliary gland origin commonly lie beside bile ducts, including near the hepatic hilum. The published literature includes extrahepatic as well as intrahepatic lesions.

review.title: What counts as dilation?
review.text: Bosselmann and colleagues used 2 mm to distinguish ectasia from cysts in their study of end-stage alcohol-related liver disease. Their cutoff describes that study’s histologic classification. A systematic review documented a wider range of cyst sizes across the included studies.

review.title: What imaging can show
review.text: Cysts can appear as a series of small fluid-filled structures alongside the ducts. Their position and lack of visible communication with the biliary lumen help distinguish them from duct dilation. An ex vivo OCT study investigated tissue microstructure at a different scale from conventional imaging.

review.title: Clinical context
review.text: Peribiliary cysts are often incidental. The systematic review describes cases associated with underlying liver disease, and a smaller subset with obstruction or diagnostic confusion. Case reports can overrepresent unusual or symptomatic presentations.

review.title: Dilation versus mimics
review.text: A cyst adjacent to a bile duct, a dilated bile duct, and a lesion arising inside a duct are different structures. Anatomic location and communication with the duct help frame the differential. A single size measurement provides limited information.

review.title: Open research questions
review.text: Longitudinal data and consistent definitions would improve comparisons across populations. For OCT studies, useful next steps include testing reproducibility, quantifying agreement with histology, and evaluating performance in the intended setting.

topics.title: Peribiliary glands and their blood supply
topics.text: The peribiliary vascular plexus supplies the bile duct wall. A donor-biopsy study found that injury to deeper peribiliary glands and the surrounding vascular plexus was more common in grafts that later developed non-anastomotic strictures.

topics.title: Ischemia–reperfusion injury
topics.text: Histologic injury to donor bile ducts before implantation provides a way to study later biliary complications. The association between deeper gland injury and subsequent strictures makes the gland compartment a target for transplant research.

topics.title: Allograft rejection
topics.text: The Banff Working Group describes patterns of bile duct injury in liver allograft rejection and considers alternative explanations for the findings. This raises a research question about how to distinguish overlapping injury patterns.

topics.title: Cytomegalovirus and biliary complications
topics.text: Observational studies have reported differing associations between cytomegalovirus infection and biliary complications after transplantation. One retrospective study did not find an independent association with non-anastomotic strictures. Differences in definitions and cohorts limit comparison.

topics.title: Non-anastomotic biliary strictures
topics.text: These strictures occur away from the surgical connection. Donor-biopsy work links them to gland and microvascular injury, supporting further study of how the bile duct epithelium repairs after transplantation.

topics.title: Comparing evidence on biliary injury
topics.text: Donor-biopsy studies, rejection criteria, and imaging studies answer different questions. When comparing findings, consider the sampled tissue, how the outcome was defined, and whether the measurements were made ex vivo or in the intended clinical setting.
